title: Mortgage revelations put banks in the spotlight
full_text:
It’s early days in reporting season and already the market has had a nasty wake-up call.
A sobering outlook for housing credit growth from the nation’s second-largest bank sent its stock price down much as 5.8 per cent to a five-week low of $35.71 on Monday.
Westpac’s quarterly update showed its average monthly mortgage applications fell 11 per cent in the June quarter, and 20 per cent since the May 12 federal budget. Investor applications were down 26 per cent.
The bank now expects housing credit growth to slow from 6.8 per cent this financial year to just 4.7 per cent in FY27. Investor loan growth is forecast to drop from 9.1 per cent to 4.5 per cent and stay there through FY28. It points to a sharp adjustment in the mortgage book once the full impact of higher interest rates and the federal budget’s property tax changes bites.
As Morgan Stanley’s banks team puts it, the changes to property-related tax concessions since May mean “much more disclosure on trends in the mortgage market is required”.
Investors want to know the level and mix of post-budget applications, and what it means for growth going forward.
The timing could not be worse for a sector trading at premium multiples. Bank shares have had a great run in recent weeks.
Helped by a pullback in mining stocks, steady demand from industry super funds, and perhaps some safe-haven buying during the memory chip sell-off that hit South Korea’s market, the ASX 200 banks index rallied about 15 per cent between June 9 and August 6.
That resulted in the average 12-month forward price-to-earnings multiple for the big four rising to 20 times against a long-run average that is closer to 12 times.
It’s a big gap to justify, especially with credit growth slowing rapidly. At the same time the ASX 200 surged 6 per cent over the past fortnight, hitting a record high of 9296.6 points largely because of the strength in banks and a rebound in mining stocks.
Westpac’s sell-off looks to have stalled that rally for now. Morgan Stanley is cautious about Commonwealth Bank specifically, saying its premium valuation is “difficult to justify given a more challenging outlook for the Australian banking sector”.
The broker foresees earnings growth moderating as mortgage competition intensifies and system credit growth slows. It expects “meaningful downside” to its base case value and price target.
Updates from other banks over the next week will show whether Westpac’s numbers are a one off.
CBA reports on Wednesday, ANZ has a trading update on Thursday, and NAB will update the market on Monday. All eyes will be on whether they confirm the same slide in mortgage demand.
It comes as Morgan Stanley predicts a structural shift whereby property investment will become less dominated by high-income earners using leverage and tax losses to chase capital growth on low-yield assets. New investors will need to focus more on cashflow discipline, while those chasing tax breaks will be pushed towards new housing supply rather than established homes.
Over time, this could mean lower average leverage across the mortgage book and a rental market that behaves more like an income investment than a speculative one. That’s a healthier housing market in some ways. But it’s a slower one for bank lending growth in the medium term.
None of this means the banks are heading for a crisis. Westpac’s underlying business is solid. Net profit was up 2 per cent for the quarter and margins are holding steady at 1.89 per cent.
But solid earnings and a cheap valuation are two very different things. If the other banks echo Westpac’s message on slowing housing credit and falling mortgage applications, the rerating of bank shares back towards long-run normality could have further to run. Investors who piled into banks during the recent rally as a safe haven, or simply because the momentum was too strong to ignore, may now need to ask a harder question: are the earnings assumptions behind those valuations still valid once the housing market properly slows down?
